 7   4. DISCUSSION

 8                                                        oo
            The main objective of this study was to verify whether changes in skin
                                                            f
 9   temperature can be compared with the inflammatory physiological changes observed

10                                          re -p
     after exercise protocols in trained individuals. Based on the eligibility and selection

11
                                                  r
     criteria adopted, as shown in figure 1, the scarcity of studies relating infrared

12

13
                                    lP
     thermography to changes in athletes' biological markers is surprising. Which awakens

     us to a field of study that still needs to be explored in depth.

14
                       urna
            Observing the years of publication of the studies selected for this systematic

15   review, we noticed that the oldest study is from 2014 (Bandeira et al), followed later

16
               Jo
     by Fernandes et al, which published later, in 2017. Two years later, Perez -Guarner et

17   al, presents a study in 2019. In 2021, we already see two publications (Korman et al

18   and Rojas-Valverde et al). We believe that this low number of published studies can

19   be explained by the fact that older infrared thermography equipment had low image

20   resolution, high cost, and difficulty in moving the equipment. In addition, there was a

21   lack of methodological standards, limiting the veracity of the studies (Elliot, 1999).

22   However, nowadays this equipment has evolved and has become portable, with high

23   thermal sensitivity and image resolution, which guarantees greater precision in the

24   measurements obtained during the evaluation (Côrte & Hernandez, 2016). In this way,
                                                                                            11


 1   this equipment has become an interesting alternative for measuring training load,

 2   identifying and preventing injuries, and the proposal for identifying thermoregulatory

 3   changes before, during and after exercise (Pinheiro et al, 2021). For Tanda (2016),

 4   more modern thermal imaging devices are more suitable for mapping the distribution

 5   and evolution of skin temperature during exercise.

 6            The diversity in the results presented among the five studies selected for this

 7   systematic review is due to the variety of sports modality explained. In two studies,

 8

 9
                                                          oo
     participating athletes practice team sports, such as Rugby (Bandeira et al, 2014) and

                                                            f
     Football (Fernandes et al, 2017). The other selected studies present individual

10
                                            re
     characteristics, being: Half-marathon (Perez-Guarner, 2019), Sprinter (Korman et al,

                                               -p
11

12
                                                  r
     2021) and Marathon (Rojas-valverde, 2021). However, each sport has its own

     particularities and physiological characteristics.

13
                                    lP
              The increase in temperature identified in studies by infrared thermography in

14                      urna
     different parts of the body shortly after or days after physical activity determines that

15   blood flow is reestablished to the injured muscle in order to supply immune cells, which

16               Jo
     makes it necessary for muscle regeneration and with the objective of removing the

17   accumulation of metabolites (Uchôa et al, 2018). Therefore, the results analyzed from

18   the selected studies seem to be in line with the findings of the study by Uchôa et al,

19   (2018) in which they conclude that the muscle recovery process is characterized by

20   increasing heat in that specific muscle that received the demand from the exercise,

21   this, however, happens due to the high rate of metabolism and blood flow (Gatt et al,

22   2015).

23            However, in the study proposed by Fernandes and collaborators (2017), skin

24   temperature and CK were moderately related in all ROIs analyzed. And these findings
                                                                                           12


 1   revealed that skin temperature is markedly affected and related to the level of

 2   inflammation triggered by the football match. However, 48 hours after a football match

 3   has not yet been shown to be an efficient amount of time to recover from match-

 4   induced muscle damage and concomitant inflammation caused by repeated football

 5   matches. Since these athletes are constantly exposed to a series of physical overloads

 6   through training and official games that promote physiological changes, such as

 7   fatigue, increased concentration of pro-inflammatory enzymes that are harmful to the

 8   muscles (Bishop, Jones & Woods, 2008), in addition to increased circulating blood

 9
                                                        oof
     flow in the region (Fernandez-Cuevas et al, 2015). In the study by Rojas-Valverde et

10

11
                                          re
     al (2021), which aimed to evaluate the effect of basal temperature after a marathon

                                             -p
     held in an uncontrolled and hot environment, it was concluded that the condition

12
                                                r
     caused an increase in basal temperature 24 hours after the marathon. This result was

13                                 lP

14

15
                      ur
     physiological processes due to the peripheral vasodilation promoted, and this can be

                        na

16   importance, since the study did not obtain a relationship or correlation with biological

17   markers.
                Jo
18         However, the study by Perez-Guarner (2019) proved to be different, where

19   during the assessment 24 hours before the half marathon race, the athletes showed

20   an increase in basal temperature, not only that, the half marathon resulted in

21   physiological stress, which which can be seen in the variables analyzed (blood

22   markers, jumping performance and perception of fatigue and pain). However, average

23   skin temperature increased the day before the half marathon race and 48 hours after

24   the race. The explanation given by the authors referring to the increase in basal

25   temperature in the assessment 24 hours before the race is that there was an increase
                                                                                          13


 1   in the environmental temperature of the city where the experiment was carried out.

 2   However, another possible question is presented by the study by Formenti & Merla

 3   (2017), which according to them, there may be activation of the sympathetic activity of

 4   the autonomic nervous system.

 5         The research by Korman and collaborators (2021) appears to be somewhat

 6   particular, as it relates the basal temperature of the lower limbs with the CK of men

 7   and women in a camp of ten consecutive days of training, and analyzed them in two

 8

 9
                                                       oo

                                                         f
     be able to interfere with the skin temperature of the lower limbs and CK. As a result,

10
                                          re

                                             -p
11

                                                r

14

15
                      ur

                        na

16

17

     to favorably affect physical performance, due to a greater heat storage capacity,

18   (Korman et al, 2021).

19         The study by Bandeira et al. (2014) presents a particularity: the authors report

20   a certain limitation in the results found, since the measurement of basal temperature

21   and CK occurred only 48 hours after a training session and 48 hours after a game.

22   This makes it difficult to correlate these two techniques, since there is no assessment

23   before the training session and the game, which could clarify the interpretation and

24   show more accurately whether or not serum CK levels and skin temperature

25   increased. This difficulty encountered by the authors in relating skin temperature to
                                                                                             14


 1   biomarkers is also shown by the sport analyzed, Rugby. This is a sport where there is

 2   diversity in the data, where muscle injuries occur both due to trauma and the intensity

 3   of the activities performed. This impacts the time of release and activity of CK, since

 4   they depend mainly on the type and intensity of the exercise performed, as described

 5   in the study by (Brancaccio, Lippi & Maffulli, 2010). However, not all studies evaluate

 6   athletes for a few days as a way of controlling the evolution of basal temperature and

 7   biological markers. This can be exemplified in the study by Moreira and collaborators

 8   (2019) in which he evaluated 23 judo athletes with a specific test for the modality, and

 9
                                                         oof
     there he evaluated the temperature of 26 regions and blood lactate to compare them

10

11
                                           re
     with each other, the chosen period it was in the pre-test and 5,10 and 15 minutes after

                                              -p
     the judo exercise intervention. A similar procedure was found in the research by Tuono

12
                                                 r
     and collaborators (2021), where they evaluated the basal temperature of the lower

13                                 lP
     limbs of athletes practicing duathlon sprints at three moments, before the competition,

14

15
                      ur
     immediately after and 10 minutes after the competition. However, they did not

                        na

17
               Jo
            Despite this, the low quantity, the divergence of study protocols and the

18   biological markers, triggered in the body after physical activity. Still, this makes

20   studies may add new stages of assessing body temperature and biological markers,

22


23   5. CONCLUSION
                                                                                          15


 1         Infrared thermography appears to be a very reliable, safe and non-invasive

 2   method for demonstrating the thermal pattern of the skin when used for injury

 4   effectiveness of infrared thermography in correlating with biological markers of muscle

 5   damage. Thus, the use of infrared thermography as a tool combined with clinical

 6   examination techniques can be a complement to clinical evaluations and support

 7   professionals' decisions. However, there are still many doubts regarding the

 8   effectiveness and accuracy of thermal responses in sports, which opens precedents

 "evidenceSummary":"PRISMA systematic review (PROSPERO CRD42022385463) of five experimental studies with 81 trained athletes aged 18 or older, including rugby, soccer, sprint and distance runners of both sexes, comparing infrared thermography skin temperature with blood creatine kinase (CK) or lactate after training, matches or races. Four studies found no meaningful correlation or predictive relationship between skin temperature and biomarkers, and one reported a moderate relationship between skin temperature and CK after two consecutive soccer matches.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only five small studies (10-21 athletes each) were included, with different protocols, time points and cameras, and most were rated uncertain on the reference standard domain of QUADAS-2. The review also reports 55 men and 26 women in the text but 60 men and 21 women in Table 1, and its discussion of the half-marathon study conflicts with Table 2.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the review's statement that infrared thermography is reliable for injury screening as shown by these studies, when the five included studies compared skin temperature with biomarkers and did not test screening accuracy.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2025,
   "citation":"Nobre TL, Rocha LY, Carbone PO, Grassi MCF, de Oliveira Júnior R, Caperuto EC. The Relationship of Infrared Thermography With the Identification of Changes in Biological Markers After Exercise: A Systematic Review. Journal of Bodywork & Movement Therapies. 2025 (in press).",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.jbmt.2025.04.018",
   "abstract":"This PRISMA systematic review asked whether changes in skin temperature measured by infrared thermography match the inflammatory and muscle-damage changes seen after exercise in trained people. Five studies were included, and the authors found few studies linking the method to biomarkers, with weak or inconsistent associations.",
   "tldr":"Infrared thermography is used widely in sport, but it has been tested against blood muscle-damage markers in only five small studies, and most found no clear link. Use it as a screening aid alongside clinical examination, not as a substitute for CK or lactate.",
   "methods":"A PRISMA systematic review registered in PROSPERO (CRD42022385463), with searches of PubMed, MEDLINE, LILACS, SciELO, SPORTDiscus and Embase in January 2023 and no language or date restriction. Two reviewers screened full texts, and the included studies were experimental trials of trained athletes of both sexes over 18 that measured infrared skin temperature alongside CK or lactate. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2.",
   "findings":"Five studies were included, with 81 athletes in total (10 to 21 per study) from rugby, soccer, sprint and distance running. Bandeira et al. (2014, rugby) found no correlation between skin temperature variation and serum CK. Fernandes et al. (2017, soccer) found skin temperature and CK moderately related in all regions after two consecutive matches, with CK higher 48 h after the second match. Korman et al. (2021, sprinters) found no correlation between leg skin temperature and CK over a 10-day camp. Perez-Guarner et al. (2019, half-marathon) reported that a regression model could not predict physiological stress from skin temperature, and Table 2 reports no skin temperature increase after the race. Rojas-Valverde et al. (2021, marathon) found higher skin temperature the day after the race but no correlation with muscle damage markers.",
   "limitations":"The authors note the small number of studies, differing protocols and sports, and few time points, which made correlation hard to establish. Most studies were rated uncertain on the reference standard domain of QUADAS-2. The text reports 55 men and 26 women, but Table 1 gives 60 men and 21 women, and the discussion says skin temperature rose 24 h before and 48 h after the half-marathon while Table 2 reports no post-race rise, so the table values are used here. Bandeira et al. measured only 48 h after training or a match, so no pre-session baseline existed.",
   "practicalImplications":"Staff can use infrared thermography to flag skin-temperature asymmetry for clinical follow-up, as the authors suggest, together with clinical examination. On current evidence it should not be used as a stand-in for CK or lactate to judge muscle damage after training or matches. Future protocols should measure skin temperature and biomarkers before and after sessions.",
   "athleteDev":"Performance Application: skin temperature changes were seen after matches, marathons and camps, but they did not consistently track muscle-damage markers. Using it to periodize training load would need baseline measures and a validated link to load, which these studies do not provide.",
   "rtp":"Return to Sport Application: no included study examined injury recovery, rehabilitation or return to play, so the review cannot inform return-to-play decisions. Its use for injury screening is discussed by the authors but not tested in these studies."
 }
}

(2019, half-marathon) reported that a regression model could not predict physiological stress from skin temperature, and Table 2 reports no skin temperature increase after the race.
